coverage: This is a closed-universe matter. Each step forbids any authority, facts, or data beyond the listed uploads and requires citations by exact document name with page and paragraph, so I judged criteria first against the uploads. I compared real law only where a criterion's correctness depends on it, or where the uploads themselves point to it. I read the pinned original PDFs (rendered page images) for the comparator memorandum and the Award to confirm the extractions; they match. Read in full: the assignment-4 instruction and the accumulated prompts, all eleven uploads including the Bell supplemental disclosure, and all 9 criteria including one penalty. Law checked: FOP, 973 A.2d at 178-79 (uploaded copy read in full; CourtListener text checked by passage search), for the rule that objections not first urged before the Board will not be considered (citing D.C. Code § 1-617.13(b)), which supports criterion 4. Criteria reviewed with no defect established (6 of 9): 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7. The Kucera distinctions (no injury; negotiated settlement with waiver of grievance rights) and the outside-the-record point are well grounded in Bell memo ¶¶ 2-4.

findings.title: 28 of 73 points for spotting an immaterial date error in the Bell memo
findings.explanation: Criterion 8 requires the response to identify that the Bell memo 'misdates the comparator memorandum it references': Bell ¶ 1 refers to the 'April 17, 2024 comparator memorandum,' while the Britt memorandum is dated April 11, 2024. The discrepancy is real. But the prompt asks how the supplemental comparator changes the scope, burden, preservation, contrary-to-law, and public-policy analysis, and whether the comparator can be considered on review. The misdating affects none of those questions. The justification grounds the item only in the general instruction to 'Support every point with page and paragraph citations.' A careful associate citing the Britt memo by its exact listed name (which includes 'Apr. 11, 2024') might notice the error, and noting it is good practice. But silence on it is not wrong on any point the prompt asked, and the item outweighs every substantive criterion in the assignment (the next largest are 16 points). Reasonable graders would differ on whether this is diligence or an unrequested gotcha.

evidence.quote: a closed disciplinary case involving a firearm discharge that was not included in the Disciplinary Review Division’s April 17, 2024 comparator memorandum.

findings.suggested_fix: Reduce the weight to a small diligence credit, or fold it into a citation-accuracy item.

findings.title: The -16 penalty text ('holds each of MPD's arguments') is not intelligible as written
findings.explanation: Penalty misfire: criterion 5 deducts 16 points if a response 'Mentions that the supplemental comparator document holds each of MPD's arguments.' 'Holds' has no clear meaning here. It might mean the comparator leaves every argument intact ('all arguments hold'), that it supports every argument, or that it bears on every argument. The justification ties it to the prompt's request to state 'which of MPD's contrary-to-law arguments survive unchanged, which are weakened, and whether the public policy argument is affected.' A judge applying the text literally could penalize a response that correctly says the comparator bears on each argument in some way (weakening factor six, leaving public policy unaffected), or could fail to penalize the intended error (saying no argument is weakened). The grading effect is unpredictable.

evidence.quote: Mentions that the supplemental comparator document holds each of MPD's arguments.

findings.suggested_fix: Reword: 'States that the supplemental comparator leaves all of MPD's contrary-to-law arguments unaffected.'

findings.title: 'Public policy argument is unaffected' rejects a defensible answer, given that MPD itself retained an officer after a similar shooting
findings.explanation: Criterion 9 (+3) requires the response to state that 'the public policy argument is unaffected by the supplemental comparator because it does not depend on comparator evidence.' Legally, the comparator is outside the record, and the public-policy test under W.R. Grace and Misco looks to whether enforcing the award violates a well-defined and dominant policy. On that view the criterion is right. But Kucera is MPD's own decision to keep an officer who, off duty, armed herself, confronted an unarmed suspected car burglar, and fired at him without calling 9-1-1, with a 40-day suspension. MPD's central public-policy claim is that 'reinstating an officer who shot an unarmed, non-threatening man contravenes a dominant public policy.' A careful advisor could reasonably say the comparator undercuts that claim in practice and creates disclosure and credibility risk, even if it cannot formally be considered. The prompt's phrasing ('whether the public policy argument is affected at all') invites that judgment. The criterion takes one reasonable side and fails the other.

evidence.quote: Sergeant Kucera retrieved her service pistol from inside her home, advanced to the driveway, identified herself as a police officer, and fired one round at the man as he turned toward her. ... Sergeant Kucera accepted a 40-day suspension without pay
reinstating an officer who shot an unarmed, non-threatening man contravenes a dominant public policy against the unjustified use of deadly force by police officers.

authorities.citation: W.R. Grace & Co. v. Local Union 759, 461 U.S. 757, 766 (1983) (uploaded)
authorities.proposition: A public policy invoked to refuse enforcement must be well defined and dominant, ascertained by reference to laws and legal precedents.

findings.suggested_fix: Credit either 'legally unaffected because outside the record and not comparator-dependent' or a reasoned explanation of practical effects on the policy argument.
